# The spectral transfer equation {#sec-spectral-rte}

## The physical question {#sec-spectral-rte-question}

@sec-overview defined the observable as an integral of the spectral angular
intensity $I_\lambda(\mathbf x,\hat s,t)$ over the arrival direction, the
wavelength and a time bin. This chapter answers the question that leaves open:
what equation does $I_\lambda$ obey?

The unknown is a function of seven arguments --- three of position, two of
direction, one of time, one of wavelength --- and the direction is the argument
that cannot be dropped. It would be enough to track the photon density if the
observable were the amount of light at a point. It is not: a module accepts
light from some directions and rejects it from others, and the fraction of
arriving light that it accepts depends on how the arrival directions are
distributed. Two fields with the same photon density at the module and
different angular shapes give different counts. The angular argument is carried
because the detector reads it.

The mechanisms acting on the photons divide in two, and the division organises
everything that follows. Absorption *removes* photons; a source *creates*
them; these change the total number. Scattering does neither: it moves a photon
from one direction to another at the same place and the same instant. Writing
the loss from a direction and the gain into it as two separate terms, which
must cancel when integrated over all directions, is what makes the equation a
conservation law with absorption --- and it gives the sharpest check available
on any implementation of it (@sec-spectral-rte-checks).

Each wavelength is solved on its own because scattering in water is elastic on
the scale that matters here: a photon changes direction without changing
wavelength, so no term in the equation couples $\lambda$ to $\lambda'$. The
wavelengths meet only in the source that creates them and in the final integral
over $\lambda$ that produces the observable.

Finally, $I_\lambda$ is an expectation. It describes the mean photon
distribution of an ensemble of events, not one realisation of a random walk.
Nothing below is a statement about an individual photon history; what is
computed is the average that such histories would approach.

## Assumptions and definitions {#sec-spectral-rte-assumptions}

The medium is homogeneous, unbounded and stationary; its optical coefficients
are given and are not modified by the light itself. Between interactions
photons travel in straight lines at constant speed. Intensities add, and
coherent interference is neglected --- the kinetic description applies at
scales where this holds [see e.g. Arridge & Schotland, *Inverse Problems*
**25**, 123010 (2009)].

The notation is the one fixed in @sec-overview. Position $\mathbf x$, time $t$,
wavelength $\lambda$, and the unit vector $\hat s$ giving the direction in
which a photon *travels*. On the sphere of directions
$\mathrm d\Omega=\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$ and
$\int_{S^2}\mathrm d\Omega=4\pi$. The spectral angular intensity is defined by
$$
\mathrm dN=\frac{I_\lambda(\mathbf x,\hat s,t)}{v_g(\lambda)}\,
\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega\,\mathrm d\lambda ,
$$ {#eq-spectral-intensity}
repeating @eq-overview-intensity: the expected number of photons in the spatial
volume $\mathrm d^3x$, travelling into the solid angle $\mathrm d\Omega$ about
$\hat s$, with wavelength in $\mathrm d\lambda$ about $\lambda$. The factor
$1/v_g$ is what distinguishes the intensity from the phase-space density
$f_\lambda=I_\lambda/v_g$; @sec-spectral-rte-exercises asks for both forms of
the equation.

| Symbol | Meaning | Units |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $I_\lambda$ | spectral angular intensity | photon $\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm{ns}^{-1}\mathrm{sr}^{-1}\mathrm{nm}^{-1}$ |
| $f_\lambda=I_\lambda/v_g$ | spectral angular photon density | photon $\mathrm m^{-3}\mathrm{sr}^{-1}\mathrm{nm}^{-1}$ |
| $\mu_a(\lambda)$ | absorption coefficient | $\mathrm m^{-1}$ |
| $\mu_s(\lambda)$ | scattering coefficient | $\mathrm m^{-1}$ |
| $\mu_t=\mu_a+\mu_s$ | extinction coefficient | $\mathrm m^{-1}$ |
| $n_{\rm ph}(\lambda)$ | phase refractive index | dimensionless |
| $n_g(\lambda)$ | group refractive index | dimensionless |
| $v_g=c_0/n_g$ | group speed | $\mathrm m\,\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$ |
| $c_0=0.299792458$ | vacuum speed of light | $\mathrm m\,\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$ |
| $q_\lambda$ | spectral volumetric creation rate per direction | photon $\mathrm m^{-3}\mathrm{ns}^{-1}\mathrm{sr}^{-1}\mathrm{nm}^{-1}$ |
| $p_g(\hat s,\hat s')$ | density of the outgoing direction given the incoming one | $\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$ |
| $g$ | mean cosine of scattering | dimensionless |

Over a short path $\mathrm d\ell$ the probabilities of absorption and of
scattering are $\mu_a\,\mathrm d\ell+o(\mathrm d\ell)$ and
$\mu_s\,\mathrm d\ell+o(\mathrm d\ell)$. The reciprocals $1/\mu_a$ and
$1/\mu_s$ are the absorption and scattering lengths of the two processes taken
separately; $1/\mu_t$ is the mean free path to the first interaction of either
kind.

**The order of the arguments of the phase function is a convention and it is
fixed here.** In $p_g(\hat s,\hat s')$ the *first* argument is the outgoing
direction and the *second* is the incoming one, and the normalisation is on the
outgoing direction:
$$
p_g(\hat s,\hat s')\ge0,\qquad
\int_{S^2}p_g(\hat s,\hat s')\,\mathrm d\Omega=1
\quad\text{for every }\hat s' .
$$ {#eq-phase-normalisation}
With this convention $p_g$ is a conditional probability density: given that a
photon travelling along $\hat s'$ scatters, @eq-phase-normalisation says it
must leave in *some* direction. Every cancellation in
@sec-spectral-rte-checks rests on it.

### The two refractive indices {#sec-spectral-rte-indices}

Water is dispersive, and the two refractive indices that follow from that enter
two different parts of the calculation. Keeping them apart is not pedantry: at
the distances of a neutrino telescope, confusing them costs more than a time
bin (@sec-spectral-rte-example).

The transport operator contains **only** the group index. A pulse travels at
the group speed, so the coefficient of the time derivative is
$$
\frac{1}{v_g(\lambda)}=\frac{n_g(\lambda)}{c_0},
$$ {#eq-group-speed}
and $n_{\rm ph}$ appears nowhere in @eq-spectral-rte below. The phase index
governs the *emission*: the Cherenkov condition $\beta n_{\rm ph}(\lambda)>1$,
the cone half-angle $\cos\theta_C=1/(\beta n_{\rm ph})$ and the spectral yield
all carry $n_{\rm ph}$ and no $n_g$. The derivation of that source is
@sec-cherenkov-source; what matters here is that the two indices belong to two
different operators.

The code states the same split structurally rather than by comment. The
spectral medium tabulates all four wavelength-dependent quantities, but
`SpectralMedium.band(lambda)` --- the call that produces the monochromatic
medium the transport solver actually receives --- constructs a
`lighthit.medium.Medium` whose fields are
$$
(\mu_a,\ \mu_s,\ g,\ n_g,\ \lambda,\ \text{provenance}),
$$
with **no** phase index among them. A solver holding a `Medium` therefore
cannot use $n_{\rm ph}$ even by accident: it does not have it. The phase index
is carried separately, on the source side, and reaches the arithmetic through
`SpectralLightElements.photon_density_per_nm`, which takes it as an explicit
argument. @sec-spectral-rte-example measures that the band really does omit it.

## Derivation {#sec-spectral-rte-derivation}

Fix a wavelength and a direction. Take a volume $W$ at rest with outward normal
$\hat n$, and count the photons inside it whose direction lies in a narrow
element $\mathrm d\Omega$ about $\hat s$. Six contributions change that number,
and the equation is their sum. Every term below has units
$\text{photon}\,\mathrm m^{-3}\mathrm{ns}^{-1}\mathrm{sr}^{-1}\mathrm{nm}^{-1}$;
that is the dimensional check, and it is worth repeating at each line.

**1. Accumulation.** The number in $W$ within $\mathrm d\Omega$ is
$\mathrm d\Omega\int_W(I_\lambda/v_g)\,\mathrm d^3x$ by
@eq-spectral-intensity, so the rate at which it grows is
$$
\frac{1}{v_g}\,\partial_tI_\lambda
$$
per unit volume. Units: $(\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm{ns})\times$
$\text{photon}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm{ns}^{-2}\mathrm{sr}^{-1}\mathrm{nm}^{-1}$,
as required.

**2. Streaming across the boundary.** In time $\mathrm dt$ the photons crossing
an area element $\mathrm dA$ with normal $\hat n$ come from a cylinder of
volume $v_g\,\mathrm dt\,\mathrm dA\,(\hat s\cdot\hat n)$, so the signed
outward flow is $I_\lambda\,\hat s\cdot\hat n$ per unit area and time. The net
loss from $W$ is the closed surface integral of that, and the divergence
theorem at fixed $\hat s$ turns it into a volume integral of
$$
\hat s\cdot\nabla I_\lambda .
$$
The two terms so far are not two mechanisms but one: together they say that,
left alone, the intensity is constant along a ray.

**3. Absorption.** In time $\mathrm dt$ a photon covers $v_g\,\mathrm dt$, and
the absorption probability over that path is $\mu_a v_g\,\mathrm dt$. Out of
the phase volume $\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega$ absorption therefore removes
$\mu_a v_gf_\lambda=\mu_aI_\lambda$ photons per unit volume, direction and
time:
$$
-\,\mu_aI_\lambda .
$$
An absorbed photon leaves the field being modelled and does not come back.

**4. Scattering out of the chosen direction.** By the same counting, photons
scatter out of $\hat s$ at the rate
$$
-\,\mu_sI_\lambda .
$$
A scattered photon does **not** disappear. It is removed from $\hat s$ here and
returned in another direction by the next term; for a continuous phase function
the probability of scattering into exactly the original direction is zero, and
the finite angular bin that a detector integrates over is handled correctly by
the gain term.

**5. Scattering into the chosen direction.** Out of the incoming element
$\mathrm d\Omega'$, photons scatter at the rate
$\mu_sI_\lambda(\hat s')\,\mathrm d\Omega'$ per unit volume, and a fraction
$p_g(\hat s,\hat s')\,\mathrm d\Omega$ of them leaves into the outgoing element
under consideration. Summing over all incoming directions,
$$
+\,\mu_s\int_{S^2}p_g(\hat s,\hat s')\,
I_\lambda(\mathbf x,\hat s',t)\,\mathrm d\Omega' .
$$
Position and time are the same on both sides of this integral: scattering
changes direction locally, and the displacement between collisions is already
carried by the streaming term.

**6. Creation.** The source $q_\lambda$ is defined so that
$q_\lambda\,\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega\,\mathrm d\lambda\,\mathrm dt$
photons are created in that volume, direction, wavelength and time interval. It
carries no separate factor of $v_g$, because it is already a rate per unit
volume and time. Isotropic emission at total directional rate $q_{0,\lambda}$
means $q_\lambda=q_{0,\lambda}/4\pi$.

Collecting the six,
$$
\frac{1}{v_g}\partial_tI_\lambda+\hat s\cdot\nabla I_\lambda
=-\mu_tI_\lambda+\mu_s\mathcal K_gI_\lambda+q_\lambda ,
$$ {#eq-spectral-rte-balance}
where the direction-changing operator is
$$
(\mathcal K_gI_\lambda)(\hat s)
=\int_{S^2}p_g(\hat s,\hat s')\,I_\lambda(\hat s')\,\mathrm d\Omega' .
$$ {#eq-scattering-operator}
Moving everything that acts on $I_\lambda$ to the left,
$$
\left[\frac{1}{v_g(\lambda)}\partial_t+\hat s\cdot\nabla
+\mu_a(\lambda)+\mu_s(\lambda)-\mu_s(\lambda)\,\mathcal K_g\right]
I_\lambda=q_\lambda .
$$ {#eq-spectral-rte}
This is the equation LightHit solves. $\mathcal K_g$ is dimensionless as an
operator --- $p_g$ carries $\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$ and $\mathrm d\Omega'$ carries
$\mathrm{sr}$ --- so $\mu_s\mathcal K_g$ has the units of $\mu_s$, and every
bracketed term reduces to $\mathrm m^{-1}$ acting on $I_\lambda$.

The same equation follows along a short ray segment without any volume at all:
$$
I_\lambda(\mathbf x+\hat s\,\mathrm d\ell,\hat s,t+\mathrm d\ell/v_g)
-I_\lambda(\mathbf x,\hat s,t)
=\bigl[-\mu_tI_\lambda+\mu_s\mathcal K_gI_\lambda+q_\lambda\bigr]
\mathrm d\ell+o(\mathrm d\ell),
$$
whose left-hand side expanded to first order returns
@eq-spectral-rte-balance. The two derivations disagree nowhere, and the second
makes it plain that the left-hand side is a derivative taken *moving with the
photons*.

### The Henyey--Greenstein kernel {#sec-spectral-rte-hg}

@eq-spectral-rte holds for any normalised phase function. The model used
throughout is Henyey--Greenstein, which depends on the directions only through
$c=\hat s\cdot\hat s'$:
$$
p_g(c)=\frac{1-g^2}{4\pi\,(1+g^2-2gc)^{3/2}},\qquad -1<g<1 .
$$ {#eq-hg}
Two properties are used constantly and both are verified numerically in
@sec-spectral-rte-checks:
$$
\int_{S^2}p_g\,\mathrm d\Omega=1,\qquad
\int_{S^2}c\;p_g\,\mathrm d\Omega=g .
$$ {#eq-hg-moments}
The first is @eq-phase-normalisation; the second is what makes $g$ *the* mean
cosine rather than a shape parameter with a suggestive name. Water in a lake is
strongly forward-peaked, and the production model uses $g=0.9$: a scattered
photon keeps most of its original direction, and it takes many scatterings to
forget where it came from.

Beyond these two, the property that decides the numerical scheme is that
@eq-hg has Legendre eigenvalues $g^\ell$:
$$
2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}p_g(c)\,P_\ell(c)\,\mathrm dc=g^\ell .
$$ {#eq-hg-eigenvalues}
In words, $\mathcal K_g$ is diagonal in the angular index with eigenvalue
$g^\ell$, which is why the scattering operator never has to be stored as a
matrix and why its truncation is controlled by a geometric sequence. The
harmonic machinery that turns @eq-hg-eigenvalues into a tridiagonal linear
system belongs to @sec-angular-system and is not anticipated here;
@sec-spectral-rte-checks only measures that the eigenvalues are what they are
claimed to be.

One limitation of the current contract belongs in this chapter rather than
later. `SpectralMedium` tabulates $\mu_a$, $\mu_s$, $n_{\rm ph}$ and $n_g$
against wavelength, but takes $g$ as a **single scalar** shared by the whole
band. A measured phase function that is not of the form @eq-hg, or an
asymmetry that varies across the band, cannot be expressed in the present model
(@sec-spectral-rte-validity).

### Why the wavelengths do not mix {#sec-spectral-rte-elastic}

Every term of @eq-spectral-rte is evaluated at one wavelength. There is no
integral over $\lambda'$ anywhere, because scattering is taken to be elastic:
the direction changes, the wavelength does not. The coefficients depend on
$\lambda$, so the equation is a *different* equation for each wavelength, but
the equations are independent, and solving nine of them is solving nine
separate monochromatic problems rather than one coupled spectral problem.

The wavelengths meet in exactly two places, and neither is inside
@eq-spectral-rte. They meet in the source, because one emitting element
radiates a continuous spectrum, and they meet in the final integral over
$\lambda$ that assembles the observable @eq-overview-pe. The quadrature used
for that integral --- how many nodes, where, with what weights --- is a
property of the observable and is chosen in @sec-rte-to-pe. It has nothing to
do with the interpolation of the medium table discussed in the next section,
which is a way of *evaluating coefficients* at a requested wavelength. Reading
them as one thing is a common confusion and the two never appear in the same
formula.

One transitional remark closes the derivation. @eq-spectral-rte as it stands
is a differential equation in $\mathbf x$ and $t$ and an integral equation in
$\hat s$, which is not yet something to compute with. Because the medium is
homogeneous and unbounded, transforming in $\mathbf x$ and $t$ turns the
streaming operator into multiplication, leaving an algebraic problem on the
sphere at each $(\mathbf k,\omega)$, and the detector functional can be carried
to the right-hand side by reciprocity. That is the subject of
@sec-fourier-adjoint; nothing about it is needed here.

## The discrete algorithm {#sec-spectral-rte-algorithm}

Nothing in @eq-spectral-rte is discretised yet: the angular truncation, the
wavenumber quadrature and the frequency grid all belong to later chapters. What
*is* an algorithm at this stage is the step that turns a tabulated medium into
the monochromatic coefficients of a single spectral node --- step 2 of the map
in @sec-overview-algorithm.

1. **Validate the table.** Wavelengths must be finite, positive, strictly
   increasing and at least two of them; the four coefficient arrays must match
   them in shape; $\mu_a>0$, $\mu_s\ge0$, $n_{\rm ph}>0$ and $n_g>0$; and
   $-1<g<1$. The two refractive indices are required to be strictly positive
   for the same reason as the absorption: a zero or negative index would make
   @eq-group-speed meaningless rather than merely extreme. A table that fails
   any of these is rejected at construction, not at first use.
2. **Reject out-of-range requests.** A wavelength outside
   $[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]$ raises, *before* any interpolation is
   attempted. There is no extrapolation of optical coefficients anywhere in the
   package.
3. **Interpolate linearly.** Inside the range, each of $\mu_a$, $\mu_s$,
   $n_{\rm ph}$, $n_g$ is interpolated linearly in $\lambda$ between the two
   bracketing nodes. Linear interpolation is a modelling choice: it introduces
   no oscillation between nodes and no coefficient outside the range of the
   tabulated ones, at the price of a kink at each node.
4. **Build the monochromatic medium.** Assemble
   $(\mu_a,\mu_s,g,n_g,\lambda)$ into a `Medium`, dropping $n_{\rm ph}$, and
   derive $\mu_t=\mu_a+\mu_s$ and $v_g=c_0/n_g$ from it.

Steps 2 and 4 are the two places where this chapter's physics is enforced
rather than described: no extrapolated coefficient can enter the solver, and no
phase index can.

## Correspondence with the code {#sec-spectral-rte-code}

| Mathematics | Symbol |
|:--|:--|
| Tabulated $\mu_a(\lambda),\mu_s(\lambda),n_{\rm ph}(\lambda),n_g(\lambda),g$ | `lighthit.model.SpectralMedium` |
| Range check and linear interpolation | `lighthit.model.SpectralMedium.sample` |
| Monochromatic medium of one node | `lighthit.model.SpectralMedium.band` |
| $(\mu_a,\mu_s,g,n_g,\lambda)$, with no phase index | `lighthit.medium.Medium` |
| $\mu_t=\mu_a+\mu_s$ | `lighthit.medium.Medium.extinction_per_m` |
| $v_g=c_0/n_g$, @eq-group-speed | `lighthit.medium.Medium.speed_m_per_ns` |
| $c_0$ | `lighthit.medium.C_VACUUM_M_PER_NS` |
| $p_g(c)$, @eq-hg | `lighthit.single.hg_phase` |
| The eigenvalue $\mu_sg^\ell$ of $\mu_s\mathcal K_g$ | `lighthit.angular.angular_components`, `lighthit.angular.resolvent_rows` |
| $n_{\rm ph}$ in the emission, not in the transport | `lighthit.sources.SpectralLightElements.photon_density_per_nm` |

Two remarks on the table. First, the interpolation in `sample` is `np.interp`,
which clamps rather than extrapolates outside the data range --- so the range
check that precedes it is not a convenience but the thing that makes the
absence of extrapolation true. Removing the check would silently return the
endpoint value for any wavelength beyond the table.

Second, the angular solve never evaluates @eq-hg. What it builds is the vector
of eigenvalues
$$
\gamma_\ell=\mu_s\,g^{\ell},\qquad \ell=0,\dots,L,
$$ {#eq-hg-gamma}
an array of $L+1$ numbers, and that vector enters the linear system only
through its diagonal, as $d_0-\gamma_\ell$. The saving is not that nothing is
stored --- an array is --- but that a general scattering kernel would need an
$(L+1)\times(L+1)$ matrix and a matrix product at every wavenumber, while a
kernel diagonal in the angular index needs $L+1$ numbers and a subtraction.
@eq-hg itself is evaluated where the phase function proper is wanted: in the
once-scattered term of `lighthit.single`, and in the checks below.

## A worked number {#sec-spectral-rte-example}

The example uses public synthetic parameters: the same four-node table that
@sec-overview-example uses, so that the two chapters describe one medium. It
builds no cache, needs no compiled backend, and runs in a fraction of a second.

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
NUMBA_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  python scripts/run_spectral_rte_example.py --output .build/spectral-rte-example
```

The stored output is `docs/spectral-rte-example/summary.json`, which carries the
configuration, the library versions and the thread settings alongside every
number below.

The table is $\lambda=400,450,500,550$ nm with
$\mu_a=0.030,0.021,0.038,0.090\ \mathrm m^{-1}$,
$\mu_s=0.030,0.022,0.017,0.013\ \mathrm m^{-1}$,
$n_{\rm ph}=1.3435,1.3390,1.3360,1.3340$,
$n_g=1.3860,1.3740,1.3670,1.3630$ and $g=0.9$. The probe wavelength is
$462.5$ nm, chosen strictly inside the interval $[450,500]$ so that the
interpolation is exercised rather than a node being returned; it sits a
quarter of the way along.

| Quantity | Value at 462.5 nm |
|:--|--:|
| $\mu_a$ | $0.025250\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ |
| $\mu_s$ | $0.020750\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ |
| $\mu_t$ | $0.046000\ \mathrm m^{-1}$ |
| $n_{\rm ph}$ | $1.338250$ |
| $n_g$ | $1.372250$ |
| $v_g$ | $0.2184678\ \mathrm m\,\mathrm{ns}^{-1}$ |
| $1/\mu_a$ | $39.604\ \mathrm m$ |
| $1/\mu_s$ | $48.193\ \mathrm m$ |
| $1/\mu_t$ | $21.739\ \mathrm m$ |
| $\mu_s/\mu_t$ | $0.4511$ |

The single-scattering albedo $\mu_s/\mu_t=0.45$ says that slightly fewer than
half of all first interactions are scatterings, and the scattering length of
48 m is comparable with the module spacing of a telescope, so a photon is
neither certain to arrive unscattered nor certain to be scattered on the way.

What these lengths do **not** determine is how much of the signal at a given
module is scattered light. That ratio depends on the geometry as well ---
above all on whether the module lies on the Cherenkov cone of the event, and
on how far it is compared with $1/\mu_a$ --- and it varies by orders of
magnitude between modules of one array. @sec-overview-example shows both
extremes in a single run: one module whose charge is $56\%$ unscattered light,
and three that receive no unscattered light whatever. Neither figure can be
read off $1/\mu_s$.

The cost of confusing the two refractive indices is now a number. Over a
straight path of 100 m at this wavelength,
$$
t_g=\frac{100\,n_g}{c_0}=457.733\ \mathrm{ns},\qquad
t_{\rm ph}=\frac{100\,n_{\rm ph}}{c_0}=446.392\ \mathrm{ns},
$$
a difference of $11.341$ ns, or $2.48\%$. The production time bins of
@sec-overview-example are 20 ns wide, so substituting $n_{\rm ph}$ for $n_g$
would move the arrival by more than half a bin at 100 m and by a full bin at
200 m. This is the error that the structure described in
@sec-spectral-rte-indices exists to make impossible: the monochromatic medium
handed to the solver reports the six fields
$(\mu_a,\ \mu_s,\ g,\ n_g,\ \lambda,\ \text{provenance})$ and no phase index,
which the example asserts rather than assumes.

## Checks {#sec-spectral-rte-checks}

**Photon number is conserved by scattering.** This is the chapter's main
independent check, and it is a check on the equation rather than on the code.
Define the spectral photon-number density, flux vector and directional source
rate
$$
n_{\gamma,\lambda}=\frac{1}{v_g}\int_{S^2}I_\lambda\,\mathrm d\Omega,\qquad
\mathbf J_\lambda=\int_{S^2}\hat s\,I_\lambda\,\mathrm d\Omega,\qquad
q_{0,\lambda}=\int_{S^2}q_\lambda\,\mathrm d\Omega .
$$ {#eq-spectral-moments}
Integrate @eq-spectral-rte-balance over the outgoing direction. The first term
gives $\partial_tn_{\gamma,\lambda}$; the second gives
$\nabla\cdot\mathbf J_\lambda$; absorption gives
$-\mu_a\int I_\lambda\,\mathrm d\Omega=-v_g\mu_an_{\gamma,\lambda}$. The two
scattering terms are where the argument lives. The loss integrates to
$-\mu_s\int I_\lambda(\hat s)\,\mathrm d\Omega$. The gain is a double
integral, and exchanging the order,
$$
\mu_s\int_{S^2}\!\mathrm d\Omega\int_{S^2}\!\mathrm d\Omega'\,
p_g(\hat s,\hat s')I_\lambda(\hat s')
=\mu_s\int_{S^2}\!\mathrm d\Omega'\,I_\lambda(\hat s')
\underbrace{\int_{S^2}p_g(\hat s,\hat s')\,\mathrm d\Omega}_{=\,1
\ \text{by @eq-phase-normalisation}}
=\mu_s\int_{S^2}I_\lambda(\hat s')\,\mathrm d\Omega' ,
$$
which is the loss with the opposite sign. The two cancel identically --- for
*any* normalised phase function, not only for @eq-hg --- and what remains is
$$
\partial_tn_{\gamma,\lambda}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J_\lambda
=-v_g\mu_a\,n_{\gamma,\lambda}+q_{0,\lambda} .
$$ {#eq-spectral-number-balance}
Every term has units
$\text{photon}\,\mathrm m^{-3}\mathrm{ns}^{-1}\mathrm{nm}^{-1}$.
@eq-spectral-number-balance is local photon-number conservation with
absorption and a source, and $\mu_s$ has disappeared from it completely. That
is the diagnostic: a residual $\mu_s$ in an angular integral that should have
cancelled points at a phase-function normalisation or a quadrature weight, and
it points there before anything else.

**The Henyey--Greenstein moments.** Evaluated with a 512-node Gauss--Legendre
rule in $\cos\theta$ at $g=0.9$, @eq-hg-moments returns $1$ and $g$, and the
eigenvalues @eq-hg-eigenvalues return $g^\ell$ for $\ell=0,\dots,8$ --- $1$,
$0.9$, $0.81$, $0.729$, $0.6561$, $0.59049$, $0.531441$, $0.4782969$,
$0.43046721$. The script asserts $10^{-10}$ on the two moments and $10^{-9}$ on
the eigenvalues and fails if either is exceeded; in practice the residual comes
out near $10^{-12}$.

That residual is quoted as a bound rather than as a value on purpose. It is a
property of the quadrature and of the library that evaluates it, not of
@eq-hg, and it moves between environments; the stored summary records what the
run that produced it obtained, and a rerun elsewhere is expected to differ. It
also grows with $g$ --- at $g=0$ it sits at the level of machine precision ---
because what the rule has to resolve is a kernel that becomes sharply peaked as
$g\to1$. The companion notebook measures that trend directly.

**The interpolation is linear and is not extrapolated.** The coefficients
returned at 462.5 nm agree with a hand-written linear interpolation between the
bracketing nodes to $0$ --- bitwise, since both evaluate the same arithmetic ---
and the extinction of the monochromatic band agrees with
$\mu_a+\mu_s$ from the sample to $0$. Requesting 399 nm or 551 nm raises with
the message `wavelength outside medium range [400, 550] nm` in both directions.

**The band omits the phase index.** The fields of the monochromatic medium are
read from the object itself and checked to contain `group_index` and not
`phase_index`; the reported speed agrees with $c_0/n_g$ exactly.

All ten checks are recorded as booleans in the stored summary, and the script
exits with a failure if any of them is false, so a silent regression is not
possible.

## Range of validity {#sec-spectral-rte-validity}

@eq-spectral-rte rests on assumptions that are physical, and they are listed
separately from the numerical truncations --- the angular degree $L$, the
wavenumber cut $k_{\max}$, the frequency range $\omega_{\max}$ --- which are
not approximations of the physics but of its solution, and which belong to
@sec-angular-system, @sec-scattering-orders and @sec-validation.

- **Homogeneous and stationary medium.** The coefficients do not depend on
  position or time. A layered or time-varying medium needs a different
  treatment; the independence of the transformed problem across wavenumbers,
  used from @sec-fourier-adjoint onward, requires homogeneity specifically.
- **Straight-line propagation between collisions.** A spatially varying
  refractive index bends rays and changes the free-streaming operator.
- **Elastic scattering.** No term couples $\lambda$ to $\lambda'$. Raman
  scattering and fluorescence are outside the model.
- **Scalar intensity.** Polarisation correlations and coherent interference are
  not represented. The equation transports an intensity, not an amplitude.
- **No boundaries.** The medium is unbounded, so no boundary condition on
  incoming directions is imposed and no reflection law couples incoming to
  outgoing directions. Shadowing by the detector structure is likewise absent.
- **Coefficients independent of the intensity.** The medium does not respond to
  the light passing through it; the equation is linear in $I_\lambda$.
- **Henyey--Greenstein scattering.** The production model admits @eq-hg with a
  single scalar $g$ for the whole band. An arbitrary measured phase function,
  or a wavelength-dependent asymmetry, is not representable in the present
  contract.
- **Positive absorption, non-negative scattering.** `Medium` requires
  $\mu_a>0$ and $\mu_s\ge0$. The transfer equation itself is perfectly well
  defined at $\mu_a=0$; the strict inequality is a software contract, and a
  purely scattering medium cannot currently be expressed.
- **$-1<g<1$.** The endpoints are excluded: @eq-hg degenerates into a delta
  function as $|g|\to1$.

Outside any of these the equation is not wrong so much as inapplicable, and no
amount of numerical accuracy in solving it repairs that.

## Exercises {#sec-spectral-rte-exercises}

1. Verify the dimensions of every term of @eq-spectral-rte separately,
   starting from @eq-spectral-intensity, and confirm that $\mathcal K_g$ is
   dimensionless. Then state what changes in each term if wavelength is
   measured in metres rather than nanometres.
2. Derive the equation obeyed by the phase-space density
   $f_\lambda=I_\lambda/v_g$ from @eq-spectral-rte-balance, and explain why
   the $1/v_g$ in front of the time derivative is present in one form and
   absent in the other. Both forms count the same photons.
3. Show that in an unbounded medium with $\mu_a=0$ and no source the total
   number of photons $\int f_\lambda\,\mathrm d^3x\,\mathrm d\Omega$ is
   constant in time, given no flux at infinity. Then show for $\mu_a>0$ that it
   obeys $\mathrm dN/\mathrm dt=-v_g\mu_aN$, and say why $\mu_s$ cannot appear
   in that answer.
4. Take the limit $g\to0$ in @eq-hg and confirm that $p_0=1/4\pi$. Using
   @eq-hg-eigenvalues, say which Legendre eigenvalues survive, and explain why
   an isotropic *scattering law* does not make the intensity field isotropic:
   construct a field with $p=1/4\pi$ in which $I_\lambda$ still depends on
   $\hat s$.
5. A photon travels 200 m at 462.5 nm in the medium of
   @sec-spectral-rte-example. Compute the arrival time with $n_g$ and with
   $n_{\rm ph}$, express the difference in units of the 20 ns production time
   bin, and say at what distance the error reaches one full bin.
6. Interpolate $\mu_a$ at 462.5 nm by hand from the table of
   @sec-spectral-rte-example and confirm the value quoted there. Then explain
   what a cubic interpolation of the same table could produce that a linear one
   cannot, and why that matters for a quantity required to stay positive.

The companion notebook is `notebooks/course/01_balance.ipynb`, which draws
@eq-hg for several $g$, measures @eq-hg-moments and
@eq-hg-eigenvalues interactively, and plots the flight-time difference of
@sec-spectral-rte-example against distance. It illustrates; it is not the
source of any number quoted above.
